summary: llmcord has exactly one LLM call (llmcord.py:287) and builds its AsyncOpenAI client per Discord message from whichever provider the selected model names, so the whole migration is one decision: wrap that client with the vendored runtime. With the shipped config that puts the default model (openai/gpt-5.5) on Router -- verified live end-to-end through the real on_message(), text and image attachment, streaming translated back to Discord embeds that still finish green -- and leaves every other provider exactly where it was: OpenRouter (non-catalog model id plus openrouter: tool types), Ollama/LM Studio/vLLM (localhost, non-catalog models), and the xAI/Google/Azure providers that the shipped config lists but no model uses. The runtime stays inactive until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, so this branch is a no-op in a deployment that does not set it. Two things were needed beyond the wrap: the Dockerfile copies an explicit file list, so router_runtime.py had to be added or the Docker image would silently fall back to the provider, and the README now documents the key, the kill switch and exactly which traffic moves. On top of the migration, four improvement branches are proposed: a 50-200x cheaper default model, the conservative alternative of just dropping reasoning effort, a Router policy with a stalled-provider timeout and a product spend label, and a cross-vendor fallback to Anthropic.
reviewed: Every Router lever in ROUTER.md was checked against this app's one feature -- an interactive, user-waiting Discord reply that always streams, carries up to 25 messages of history and no output cap, and sends no function tools. Model choice and reasoning effort are where the money and the latency are (measured: a single reply cost $0.0215-$0.0281 on gpt-5.5 at high effort and $0.00008-$0.00027 on gpt-6-luna at low effort), so they became the two headline, mutually exclusive proposals. provider_timeout and a spend label are free hygiene; cross-vendor fallbacks are real resilience with a stated loss. Two levers were measured and deliberately NOT proposed: prompt_cache_key (Router already cached 3,743 of 3,746 repeated prompt tokens with no cache key, -87% on the second call, so the policy key adds nothing for OpenAI models here) and the Flex/service_tier default (left alone; billed cost varied 0.55x-1.1x of list for identical token counts, and forcing the standard tier would raise the bill with no measured latency benefit). Two choices that are the operator's and not mine are recorded as needs-decision: unlocking the vendor-direct hosts (xAI/Google/OpenRouter) onto the Router key, and capping max_output_tokens per reply. Router's web_search server tool was considered as a replacement for the OpenRouter web-search model and rejected: the runtime cannot translate a non-function tool, so llmcord would have to speak the Responses API itself.

items.title: Route the per-message OpenAI client through Router
items.summary: Wrap the AsyncOpenAI client llmcord builds per Discord message, so its openai-provider traffic goes to Router when RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set.
items.gains: The app's production LLM traffic (default model openai/gpt-5.5) is served through one Router key with per-request spend records and a feature label (metadata.feature = llmcord.py:on_message), and any catalog model can be put in config.yaml without touching code. Chat Completions is translated to Router's Responses API in both directions, streaming included, so llmcord's own request shape -- reasoning_effort, verbosity, image_url data URLs, stream=True -- is unchanged. If Router refuses before generating, the original request still reaches OpenAI once.
items.loses: Nothing for the shipped config. Two caveats for operators: extra_headers and extra_query configured on the openai provider are not forwarded on the Router-bound request (the runtime builds its own URL and header set; both still apply on the provider path), and a request Router cannot serve adds one failed Router round trip before the provider retry.
items.price: No change by itself: same models at catalog prices. Billed cost on the 8 live calls measured ran 0.55x-1.1x of catalog list price for identical token counts, so Router's per-request tier varies; the account's cost-efficient-routing default was left as is.
items.why: llmcord has one call site and builds its client dynamically from config, so the client wrap is the only change that covers every model the operator may select, routes the ones Router serves, and leaves the rest untouched -- rather than pinning the app to Router's base URL, which would have broken OpenRouter, Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, xAI, Google and Azure. The Dockerfile and README changes are part of the same decision: without the Dockerfile line the shipped image has no router_runtime.py and the import falls back to a no-op, which would look like a successful migration and route nothing.

evidence.detail: check --run --live driving the real on_message() with a stubbed Discord: text reply -> 200 /v1/responses model=gpt-5.5 feature=llmcord.py:on_message provider=openai, answer posted to the Discord embed ('Discord is a chat app for communities, gaming, and organized chaos.'); image attachment -> 200, answered the pixel question and used the <@ID> mention format.

check --run over four scenarios: openai/gpt-5.5 text and image both reached router-sim as valid /v1/responses; ollama/llama4 and openrouter/~anthropic/claude-opus-latest were kept on the provider by the runtime (reported as 'provider (runtime kept it)'), and the embed still finished with EMBED_COLOR_COMPLETE, i.e. the translated finish_reason is still 'stop'.
The repo's test command (compileall + import llmcord with asyncio.run neutralised): 2 passed, unchanged from the baseline.

plan_request() on llmcord's exact body returns kind 'chat' with model gpt-5.5, reasoning.effort=high and text.verbosity=medium translated to the Responses shape -- so the config's model parameters survive the translation.

items.title: The OpenRouter web-search model stays on OpenRouter
items.summary: openrouter/~anthropic/claude-opus-latest keeps going to openrouter.ai: its model id is not a Router catalog id and its openrouter: tools cannot be translated.
items.gains: Its web_search and web_fetch tools keep working exactly as before.
items.why: Two independent blockers: the model id llmcord sends ('~anthropic/claude-opus-latest') is not in Router's catalog, and the request carries tools of type openrouter:web_search / openrouter:web_fetch, which the runtime refuses to translate (only function tools map to Responses). Router's own web_search server tool could serve this job on a catalog model, but llmcord would have to call the Responses API itself to express it, which is a different and much larger change than this migration.

evidence.detail: check --run: the request was kept on the provider by the runtime (model=~anthropic/claude-opus-latest), and the only outbound attempt was to openrouter.ai, which the sandbox blocked.

items.title: Local servers and the unused vendor providers stay put
items.summary: ollama/llama4 (and LM Studio, vLLM, xAI, Google, Azure if an operator adds models for them) keep talking to their own endpoints.
items.gains: Self-hosted and vendor-direct deployments keep working with no Router key and no behaviour change; a model Router does not serve can never be silently redirected.
items.why: The runtime only routes api.openai.com (plus hosts explicitly unlocked, which this migration does not do), and only when the model is a Router catalog id. 'llama4' is not a catalog id and localhost is not a routed host, so the request goes to Ollama unchanged. The xAI, Google and Azure providers in config.yaml have no models in the models list, so they carry no traffic today; see nd1 for the decision about putting the vendor-direct ones on the Router key.

evidence.detail: check --run: ollama/llama4 was kept on the provider by the runtime and failed only because no Ollama server is running in the sandbox -- the request never went near Router.

items.title: Default to gpt-6-luna at low effort instead of gpt-5.5 at high
items.summary: Make openai/gpt-6-luna:vision the startup model with reasoning_effort: low, keeping gpt-5.5 in the list for /model.
items.gains: Roughly 50-200x cheaper per reply and 2-5x faster to a finished answer, measured on the real Router with llmcord's own request shape: gpt-5.5 at high effort cost $0.0215 (17.0s) and $0.0281 (21.3s) on two Discord prompts; gpt-6-luna at low effort cost $0.00008 (3.2s) and $0.00027 (10.3s). At a thousand replies a day that is roughly $20/day versus $0.15/day. Latency is the part a user watching a typing indicator actually feels.
items.loses: A smaller model answers. On the two prompts measured the substance matched (same arithmetic, same advice) but gpt-5.5's prose was wittier, which for a bot whose system prompt is 'snarky, informative but harsh' is part of the product. Low effort also means less deliberation on genuinely hard questions. Two prompts, one sample each, is not a quality evaluation -- it is a side-by-side a human should read before approving.
items.price: gpt-6-luna $0.1/$0.5 per 1M tokens versus gpt-5.5 $5/$30: 50x on input, 60x on output, plus fewer reasoning tokens at low effort.
items.why: This is the single biggest lever in the app. A Discord chat bot with a brevity-optimised system prompt was running on a $5/$30 reasoning model at high effort, with no output cap and up to 25 messages of history per request. The effort change belongs in the same decision rather than as a separate one: at high effort gpt-6-luna spent 2,513 reasoning tokens and 54.7s on the harder prompt, slower than the model it replaces, so swapping the model without lowering effort would trade cost for a worse wait. gpt-5.5 stays in the models list so an admin can switch back with /model at any time. The ':vision' suffix is llmcord's own documented mechanism: llmcord decides whether to send image attachments by matching the model name against VISION_MODEL_TAGS, which 'gpt-6-luna' does not match, and strips the suffix before calling the API.

evidence.detail: Same two prompts and the same llmcord system prompt through Router on 4 model/effort cells, n=1 per cell, answers kept for reading: gpt-5.5 high $0.0215/17.0s and $0.0281/21.3s; gpt-5.5 low $0.0158/6.1s and $0.0132/9.3s; gpt-6-luna high $0.00012/8.3s and $0.00157/54.7s; gpt-6-luna low $0.00008/3.2s and $0.00027/10.3s. Costs are Router's own usage.cost; times are to a finished answer through the recording proxy, which buffers the stream, so they are completion times, not time-to-first-token.

check --run --live through the real on_message() on this branch: text -> 200 /v1/responses model=gpt-6-luna feature=llmcord.py:on_message, and an image attachment -> 200 with the pixel answered, so the ':vision' naming keeps vision working and 'gpt-6-luna' is what reaches Router. Both embeds finished green.

Live catalog: gpt-6-luna $0.1/$0.5 (flex tier available, image input, efforts none..max) vs gpt-5.5 $5/$30. Billed cost for identical token counts varied 0.55x-1.1x of list across the 8 calls, far smaller than the 50-200x gap being decided.
Repo test command on the branch: 2 passed; the first key in config['models'] is openai/gpt-6-luna:vision.

items.title: Keep gpt-5.5 but drop reasoning effort from high to low
items.summary: The conservative alternative to i1: same model and voice, reasoning_effort: low instead of high.
items.gains: 27-53% cheaper per reply and 2-3x faster, measured live: gpt-5.5 at high effort $0.0215/17.0s and $0.0281/21.3s on two Discord prompts, at low effort $0.0158/6.1s and $0.0132/9.3s. (The $0.0158 call was billed 1.1x of list where comparable calls were billed 0.55x; on a like-for-like single attempt the saving on that prompt is nearer 60%.) Nothing about which model answers, or how it sounds, changes.
items.loses: Less deliberation on hard questions: reasoning tokens dropped from 516 to 0 on the easier prompt and from 1,034 to 312 on the harder one. Both low-effort answers stayed correct and in character, but the high-effort ones were longer and sharper.
items.price: Same model and prices; fewer billed reasoning (output) tokens per reply.
items.why: Offered because a human may well not want to change which model talks to their community, and most of the latency problem is effort rather than model: 17-21s to a finished reply is a long time to watch a typing indicator, and high effort is hard to justify for a bot whose system prompt says 'optimize for brevity'. Mutually exclusive with i1 in practice -- i1 already contains this effort change and moves the model too, so applying both is the same change twice on the same two config lines.

evidence.detail: Same two prompts through Router on gpt-5.5 at effort high and low, n=1 per cell: $0.0215/17.0s and $0.0281/21.3s at high, $0.0158/6.1s and $0.0132/9.3s at low; answers kept for reading and both remained correct and in character.
Repo test command on the branch: 2 passed; config['models']['openai/gpt-5.5'] == {'reasoning_effort': 'low', 'verbosity': 'medium'}.

items.title: Router policy: stalled-provider timeout and a product spend label
items.summary: router.policy.json adds provider_timeout: 180 and metadata.product: llmcord to this app's Router-bound requests.
items.gains: A stalled stream is Router's problem instead of the bot's: today openai-python's 600s default is the only bound, and a hung provider holds the Discord typing indicator and the message-node lock for ten minutes. metadata.product is a Ramp spend-management key, so this bot's spend is separable from anything else on the same Router key (the runtime's own metadata.feature label is kept).
items.loses: Nothing the model sees: both fields are added only to Router-bound requests, so the provider path and any Router-to-provider fallback never carry them. The residual risk is the value itself -- provider_timeout's streaming semantics (idle time between events) are documented but not measured, so a long thinking pause could in principle count against it; 180s was chosen because the slowest thinking observed in these measurements was 54.7s.
items.why: This is the one feature in the app and it is interactive and user-waiting, so an unbounded wait is the failure mode worth closing, and a label costs nothing and makes Router's spend views useful. Both are policy keys, which means they are applied by the runtime to Router-bound requests only and can be removed by reverting one commit -- no application code changes.

evidence.detail: provider_timeout: 180 on a single-model streaming /v1/responses request in llmcord's shape -> 200, streamed normally; also 200 alongside a models list.

plan_request() on llmcord's body with the compiled policy produces provider_timeout: 180 and metadata {feature: llmcord.py:on_message, product: llmcord}; with the feature label absent the policy correctly does not match. check --run through on_message(): policy 6d5d30ef loaded, request still valid at router-sim.
Repo test command on the branch: 2 passed.

items.title: Fall back to Anthropic when Router cannot serve a reply
items.summary: router.policy.json gives the chat feature fallbacks: [claude-sonnet-5-5], so Router sends a two-candidate models list instead of one model.
items.gains: A turn the primary model cannot serve is answered by another vendor instead of the user getting nothing (today the exception is logged and the embed stops orange). Measured live: a models list whose first candidate cannot serve falls through to claude-sonnet-5-5 and streams a normal answer. Cross-vendor on purpose -- a second OpenAI model does not help when OpenAI is what is down -- and vision-capable, so image turns keep a usable candidate.
items.loses: A different model, from a different vendor, sometimes answers, and the response does not say which candidate served it, so a stranger-sounding reply has no visible explanation. The fallback only covers failures before the stream starts (Router does not fall back mid-stream) and only pre-generation refusals; truncated attempts are still billed. Fall-through on real 429s and 5xx is documented by Router but was not measured here. If i1 is also applied, the fallback is 20x the primary's price while it is serving.
items.price: claude-sonnet-5-5 is $2/$10 per 1M tokens -- below gpt-5.5 ($5/$30), above gpt-6-luna ($0.1/$0.5) -- and is billed only on the turns it actually serves.
items.why: This is a user-facing chat bot with no retry logic of its own: on any pre-generation failure the user simply gets silence. A one-candidate fallback list is the cheapest resilience Router offers, costs nothing when the primary is healthy, and needs no application code. Verified that the fallback can actually serve llmcord's exact request shape, which is the real risk: llmcord sends reasoning.effort=high with text.verbosity=medium and no output cap, and Claude is strict about unknown fields and wants room to think.

evidence.detail: claude-sonnet-5-5 served llmcord's exact shape (reasoning.effort=high, text.verbosity=medium, stream, no max_output_tokens) -> 200, x-router-provider: anthropic. models=[bogus, claude-sonnet-5-5] -> 200 served by claude-sonnet-5-5 (fall-through). models=[gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-4-6] with temperature (which gpt-5.5 rejects) -> 200 served by claude-sonnet-4-6, provider anthropic. models=[gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5-5] -> 200 served by gpt-5.5, so the primary still wins when healthy.
plan_request() on llmcord's body with the compiled policy turns model: gpt-5.5 into models: [gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5-5].
Repo test command on the branch: 2 passed.

items.title: Put the vendor-direct hosts on the Router key too?
items.summary: The runtime can route xAI, Google or OpenRouter traffic (unlock_hosts) when the model is a Router catalog id; today those providers keep their own keys.
items.gains: One key and one spend record for more of the app's traffic, plus Router's levers (fallbacks, labels, timeouts) on it. x-ai/grok-4.7 and x-ai/grok-4.5 would match the catalog directly, as would google/gemini-* ids.
items.loses: Billing moves from the operator's vendor key to the Router key, silently, for models whose names happen to match the catalog -- which is a decision about money, not a technical choice, so it is not mine to make. Gemini ids are requires_byok on Router and return 403 without the caller's provider key, which would add a failed Router round trip to every Gemini call before the runtime's provider retry.
items.price: Catalog price on Router instead of the vendor's list price, for the traffic that moves.
items.why: The shipped config lists xAI, Google and Azure providers but no models for them, so nothing moves today and I did not unlock anything. If a deployment does use x-ai/grok-* or google/gemini-*, say so and the wrap becomes wrap_openai(client, unlock_hosts=[...]) -- one line, with OpenRouter deliberately left out (its ids carry a vendor prefix and never match the catalog).

evidence.detail: Not measured: no xAI or Google model is configured, so there was no traffic to test. ROUTER.md records the 403 provider_key_required behaviour for Vertex/Gemini ids as documented, not measured.

items.title: Cap the output tokens per Discord reply?
items.summary: llmcord sends no max_output_tokens, so one reply can run to the model's 128k limit.
items.gains: A bounded worst case per reply. On gpt-5.5 at $30 per 1M output tokens, a runaway turn is about $3.80 before Discord's own message splitting stops being readable; a cap of a few thousand tokens would bound it at cents.
items.loses: On a reasoning model the cap is spent on thinking first: Router returns an 'incomplete' response with no text (and reported 0 tokens in Router's own measurements), so a cap set too low turns a slow reply into an empty one. The observed turns used 264-2,820 output tokens, so a safe cap is not much below the cost it is trying to bound.
items.price: Bounds the per-reply worst case; no change to typical replies.
items.why: A guardrail with a product-visible failure mode, on a value I cannot pick for someone else's community: it depends on how long replies are allowed to be. Raised rather than applied. If you want it, the natural place is a max_tokens entry under the model in config.yaml, which llmcord already forwards as extra_body -- and it should be tested against the reasoning effort you settle on in i1/i2.

evidence.detail: Measured output tokens per reply: 264-2,820 across 8 live calls (reasoning tokens included). gpt-5.5 output is $30/1M and its catalog max_output_tokens is 128,000. ROUTER.md records that responses ending 'incomplete' on max_output_tokens returned no text.

items.title: prompt_cache_key would add nothing here: Router already caches
items.summary: A repeated 3,746-token conversation prefix was cached without any cache key, so no policy key was proposed.
items.gains: Reply chains in a Discord thread already get the discount for free -- worth knowing, because llmcord replays the whole chain (up to 25 messages) on every turn.
items.price: Second identical call: $0.0000337 instead of $0.000269, i.e. -87%, with 3,743 of 3,746 input tokens read from cache.
items.why: prompt_cache_key is the obvious lever for an app that resends a growing prefix every turn, so it was measured rather than assumed: two arms of two identical ~3.7k-token llmcord-shaped calls, one with prompt_cache_key and one without. Both arms cached the second call identically ($0.0000337 with the key, $0.0000336 without), so the key only buys provider affinity that these calls did not need, and adding it to router.policy.json would have been a lever for its own sake. Claude is the exception documented in ROUTER.md (no caching without a key) and the runtime already sets the key by itself for Anthropic-owned models, so the i4 fallback is covered too.

evidence.detail: 4 live /v1/responses calls on gpt-6-luna: without a cache key, call 1 cached 0 of 3,746 input tokens ($0.000269) and call 2 cached 3,743 ($0.0000337); with prompt_cache_key=llmcord.py:on_message, call 1 cached 0 ($0.000268) and call 2 cached 3,742 ($0.0000328). Each arm used a distinct prefix marker so it could not read the other's cache.

items.title: Flex left at the account default; billed cost varies per request
items.summary: No service_tier is forced. Identical token counts were billed 0.55x or 1.1x of catalog list price across the live calls.
items.gains: Keeping the account's cost-efficient-routing default is the cheaper setting, and llmcord always streams, which per Router's docs gives a Flex attempt a 25s deadline before a same-model standard fallback -- so the latency tail is bounded without the app doing anything.
items.price: Six of eight live calls were billed about 0.55x of catalog list price for their token counts and two about 1.1x. I did not isolate why (tier choice per request, or a retried attempt also being billed), and the variance did not track latency.
items.why: Forcing service_tier: default is the obvious move for an interactive feature, and it was rejected: it would raise the bill on every reply, ROUTER.md measures Flex latency as the same as standard on the one model where it was measured, and the slow calls observed here were slow because of reasoning effort (fixed by i1/i2), not tier. Recorded because the cost variance is worth knowing before anyone reads a single-call cost as exact -- it is well inside the 50-200x gap that decides i1, but not inside a 10% comparison.

evidence.detail: usage.cost against catalog list price for the measured token counts, 8 live calls on gpt-5.5 and gpt-6-luna: 6 at ~0.55x, 2 at ~1.10x (gpt-5.5 low/easy at 6.1s and gpt-6-luna high/hard at 54.7s), so the two outliers are not explained by latency.

items.title: At scale, the next thing to fix is a client per Discord message
items.summary: llmcord builds a fresh AsyncOpenAI client (and a fresh connection pool) for every message and never closes it.
items.gains: Reusing one client per (base_url, api_key) would give every reply a warm connection to Router instead of a new TLS handshake, and stop leaking pools -- the kind of thing that only shows up on a busy public bot, where it is both a latency tax on each reply and a socket churn problem.
items.why: Not done, because it is not a Router decision and it is not free: config.yaml is hot-reloaded per message, so a cache has to key on base_url and api_key and survive a key rotation mid-run. Flagged because the question was what I would change about this system at any scale, and this is the answer that has nothing to do with Router's levers. Wrapping is not what makes it worse -- the runtime installs its transport in place and is idempotent -- but the migration does make connection reuse worth more, since every reply now opens a connection to Router instead of to OpenAI.

evidence.detail: llmcord.py:163 constructs AsyncOpenAI inside on_message, so each Discord message gets its own httpx pool; nothing closes it. Not measured -- no load test was run.
